newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea increases defence spending in budget.
newsitem.headline: South Korea increases defence spending in budget.

text.p: The South Korean cabinet on Tuesday approved a modest overall budget increase for next year, underlining the fight against inflation, but defence spending was set to rise sharply on security concerns.
Budget spending for calendar 1997 was set at 67.78 trillion won ($82.56 billion) against 60.11 trillion won this year, according to a report on the budget by the finance ministry.
The 12.8 percent overall increase will be the smallest annual growth in the state budget since current president Kim Young-sam took office in 1993.
"This reflects the government's desire to cap inflationary pressure," said Jung Hong-sang, deputy director of the ministry's fiscal policy division.
The budget expanded by 15.6 percent in 1994, 16.7 percent in 1995 and 16.2 percent this year.
Defence spending, the biggest single spending item, will grow by 12 percent to 14.27 trillion won from this year's budget of 12.74 trillion won.
The growth in defence spending will be the highest since 1993. Annual growth for defence spending was 10.7 percent in 1996, 9.9 percent in 1995 and 9.4 percent in 1994.

"Tension is growing on the Korean peninsula and there are few signs the situation will ease in the near future. We need to spend more to strengthen our defence capabilities," Jung said in an interview.
Last month President Kim, citing "uncertainty surrounding the Korean peninsula", stressed the importance of modernising the nation's defences.
Last week's infiltration of armed North Korean troops into the South by submarine has renewed nationwide concerns about the North Korean threat.
When special accounts are included, the overall budget amounts to 71.6 trillion won, up 13.7 percent from this year's 62.96 trillion won.
The budget assumes inflation of 4.0 to 4.5 percent next year, compared with a 4.5-5.0 percent projection for this year.
Government spending will be kept at "minimum possible levels", Jung said.
The government plans a freeze on hiring next year and a clampdown on the pay of senior officials. All public utility charges will be frozen in 1997, according to the budget.
South Korea's economic growth is projected to slow to between 6.5 and 7.0 percent in 1997, compared with 7.0-7.5 percent this year, the ministry report said.
But investment in infrastructure will be expanded steadily to strengthen the nation's international competitiveness. Transport and distribution costs in Korea are among the highest in Asia.
Infrastructure investment would grow 24.4 percent to 10.14 trillion won in 1997 from 8.15 trillion won planned this year.
